title: Migrate cross-tenant delayed-job subsystem to time-wheel scheduler and add execution visibility metrics
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: The current delayed-job implementation uses per-tenant Redis sorted sets with a periodic poller that scans keys and promotes expired items. This design has caused intermittent thundering-herd behavior at billing windows, uneven latency for cross-tenant workloads, and lacks precise visibility into pending delays and execution timing. It also complicates backfill and migration to alternative transport (Kafka) for high-throughput tenants.

Goal: Replace the per-tenant polling model with a time-wheel (bucketed) scheduler that reduces timer granularity overhead, lowers Redis operational load, and provides deterministic promotion semantics. Surface per-tenant and global metrics for queued delays, promotion latency, and reschedule rates so Console + Alerting can detect regressions. Ensure a safe, reversible migration path with a dual-run mode and canary rollouts for selected tenants.

Proposed design summary:
- Implement a sharded time-wheel scheduler in the delay-service (Go). Each shard maintains an in-memory wheel of N buckets (configurable) where each bucket maps to a Redis stream key that holds job references.
- Workers subscribe to the Redis streams and claim jobs via XREADGROUP/XACK pattern to preserve at-least-once semantics. Promotion from future buckets to the immediate execution bucket is handled deterministically by advancing the wheel; no periodic scan of all tenant keys required.
- Support per-tenant buckets by namespacing within streams to keep data locality while avoiding thousands of individual sorted-set keys.
- Add visibility metrics: delay_queue.depth{tenant}, delay_queue.avg_pending_ms, delay_queue.promotion_latency_p50_p95_p99, delay_queue.reschedule_rate, and delay_queue.claim_failures. Emit tags for shard and region.
- Feature flag/dual-run: new scheduler can be enabled in a "observer" mode where it mirrors promotions to the existing queue without altering production execution, then switch to "active" mode per-tenant once stable.

Acceptance criteria:
- Promotion throughput meets or exceeds current baseline under representative load (within 10% of existing latency tail).
- Redis CPU and memory usage for delay-related keys reduced by at least 30% in canary tenants.
- Metrics above are available in Console dashboards and used by an alert (promotion_latency_p95 > 2s).
- Migration CLI exists to backfill currently-scheduled delayed jobs into the time-wheel streams for a tenant.
- Rollback path validated (switch tenant to legacy mode) without duplicate execution or lost jobs observed in canary tests.

Rollout plan: 
1. Implement time-wheel scheduler and worker changes behind a feature flag; add metrics and internal dashboard.
2. Deploy to staging; run synthetic workload against staging to validate promotion latency and prove no duplicates in consumer path.
3. Enable "observer" mode for small set of internal tenants (canary-1, canary-2). Verify metrics and resource usage for 72 hours.
4. Run migration CLI for a canary tenant; validate backfill correctness and no job loss.
5. Switch canary tenant to "active" mode and monitor for 7 days.
6. Gradually expand to high-volume tenants with repeated observation windows.
7. Finalize by deprecating legacy polling code after all tenants migrated and after a one-week stability window.

Migration steps:
- Provide a dry-run mode for the backfill tool that reports counts and top-10 long-tail delays without moving jobs.
- During active migration, mark migrated jobs with a stable migration token to avoid double-execution if legacy poller also picks them up.
- Implement idempotency keys in downstream consumers to make any accidental duplicates safe.

Testing and validation:
- Load tests with 100k delayed jobs across 200 tenants with mixed TTLs (1s..48h).
- Chaos tests: kill scheduler shard, simulate Redis failover, and ensure leader re-election promotes no-loss behavior.
- Integration tests for XGROUP/XACK semantics and consumer reclaims.

Risks & mitigations: 
- Risk: Edge-case reschedules when promotion occurs near bucket boundary may cause slightly early/late execution. Mitigation: provide configurable bucket granularity per-tenant and jitter during promotion to smooth spikes.
- Risk: Backfill might overload Redis. Mitigation: rate-limited backfill with concurrency cap and operational runbook.
- Risk: Consumer duplication during transition. Mitigation: idempotency keys and temporary dedupe window in consumers.

Open questions:
- Do we prefer Redis streams vs a hybrid approach (streams for short delays, Kafka for >24h)?
- What is the right default bucket granularity (1s vs 100ms) for high-QPS tenants?
- Should we expose a public SDK for tenants to opt into high-precision scheduling?

Design artifacts and links: 
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Timewheel+Delay+Queue+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1234
- Backfill tool prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1247

Notes: This ticket intentionally focuses on the scheduling surface and observability. Follow-up tickets will reconcile full Kafka long-retention migration and tenant-level storage configuration.
